newsitem.title: FRANCE: Taxpayer set to rescue Credit Lyonnias - again.
newsitem.headline: Taxpayer set to rescue Credit Lyonnias - again.

text.p: French taxpayers may have to ride to the rescue again of ailing state-owned bank Credit Lyonnais in order to save it from an ignominious plunge back into the red when it reports its half-year results on Thursday.

A source close to talks between the conservative government and the bank said on Monday it appeared likely a deal would be reached on a third salvage plan for the bank whose downfall was the worst banking scandal in recent French banking history.
The government and the bank, which was bailed out by the state in 1994 and 1995, have been racing against time to come up with new rescue terms before the results on Thursday.

Credit Lyonnais racked up losses of 21 billion French francs ($4 billion) between 1992 and 1994 as a result of a reckless expansion spree that briefly turned it into the world's largest bank outside Japan. It eked out a 13 million French franc profit in 1995.
The bank and the state have been in talks for months about amending last year's aid package which has become a millstone around the bank's neck.
Bank chairman Jean Peyrelevade threatened to quit in the summer if the government did not ease the burden imposed on the bank by the rescue.
Newspaper reports say under the new plan, most of the heavy costs imposed on the bank as part of an effort to make it bear some of the pain for its reckless past would be waived.

At the heart of the bank's woes is a 119-billion-franc loan the government obliged it to make at below market rates to help finance the state-owned vehicle that took over 130 billion francs of its shaky assets.
The bank has said it will lose three billion francs in funding the loan this year which analysts said could drag it into a two billion franc half-year loss.

The rescue plan is expected to opt for the scenario favoured by Peyrelevade to cut the links between the state rescue vehicle and Credit Lyonnais. This would give the bank "a fresh start," free from the burden of its past, said one source.
Under that plan, the state could cancel the impact of the loan on the bank's accounts retroactive to January 1. This could allow it to post a small half-year profit, the source said.
The government would then examine how to definitively cut the links between the so-called "bad bank" and "good bank" as of the start of next year.
Any solution, however, would have to be approved by the European Commission and pacify Credit Lyonnais's rivals, which denounced last year's rescue as too generous.
The government might have to give speed up the privatisation timetable for the bank, which it had said it hoped to sell off by 2000. The bank might also have to divest more assets.

But even without the loan, the bank still has big problems, banking analysts say. "It would be a reason to be a little more positive on the year but the core problems of the bank are a lot more dire than the loan," said one. "They are still going to have to restructure. The hard stuff is not yet done."

Its investment certificates, which make up 21 percent of the capital but carry no voting rights, have been rising in the past few weeks on hopes a deal may be near. The certificates, seen by analysts as a purely speculative play, closed at 139.2 francs on Monday, up a quarter of a percent.
But that was still far from their year high of 253.0 francs and a long way from their peak of 450 francs hit during its expansionist heyday in the late 1980s and early 1990s. ($1=5.135 French Franc)
